question:
For the second-order differential equation $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-y=0$, consider the solution family $y=C_1e^x+C_2e^{-x}$, where $C_1$ and $C_2$ are arbitrary constants.
(i) Explain why this family can represent the general solution.
(ii) If $C_1$ is fixed as $2$ while $C_2$ remains arbitrary, examine whether the resulting expression can still represent the general solution. Justify your answer.
explanation:
Step 1: Identify the arbitrary constants
The given family $y=C_1e^x+C_2e^{-x}$ contains two independent arbitrary constants, namely $C_1$ and $C_2$.
Step 2: Apply the general-solution criterion
A general solution contains as many arbitrary constants as required by the differential equation. Since the given equation is of second order, the presence of two arbitrary constants is appropriate.
Step 3: Fix one constant
If $C_1=2$, the family becomes $$y=2e^x+C_2e^{-x}.$$ Only $C_2$ remains arbitrary.
Step 4: Examine the reduced family
This expression represents only a restricted part of the original two-parameter family because one arbitrary constant has already been assigned a particular value.
Step 5: Conclusion
Therefore, $y=C_1e^x+C_2e^{-x}$ is the general solution, whereas $y=2e^x+C_2e^{-x}$ is not the complete general solution.

options.A:
(i) The family is not a general solution because it contains two constants.
(ii) Fixing $C_1=2$ gives the general solution.
options.B:
(i) The family is a general solution only when $C_1=C_2$.
(ii) Fixing $C_1=2$ does not change its general nature.
options.C:
(i) The family is a particular solution.
(ii) Fixing $C_1=2$ makes it a two-parameter general solution.
options.D:
(i) The family is a general solution because it contains two independent arbitrary constants.
(ii) Fixing $C_1=2$ leaves a restricted one-parameter family, so it is not the complete general solution.
